reference_text:
Welcome to the course. We will work through each concept carefully, connect the
ideas step by step, and use practical examples to make technical topics easier
to understand. When we introduce a new method, focus first on the problem it
solves and why it is useful. For example, in machine learning, features are the
information we give the model, while the target is what we want it to predict.
Now consider a simple question: what changes when the data contains missing
values? We will think through the reason and then look at the code. In Python,
we can inspect the data, run one small step at a time, and explain what the
result means. The goal is to understand the logic, not simply memorize syntax.

slides.title: Machine Learning & External Data
slides.transcript:
Welcome to Module 14. We’ll use the Python skills from the course to build a first end-to-end machine learning workflow.

The goal is not to master machine learning in one module. The goal is to understand the sequence: read data, define inputs and target, split the data, train a model, evaluate it, compare it with a baseline, and interpret the results carefully.

[tts-break]

Good modeling depends on good data preparation and honest evaluation, not just calling a model function.

slides.title: How to use this page
slides.transcript:
Treat each code cell as one stage of a larger workflow.

Before you run it, identify what goes into the step and what should come out. For example, a train-test split takes one dataset and produces separate training and testing subsets.

[tts-break]

Run the example, inspect shapes and outputs, and then change one setting at a time. Machine learning code becomes easier when you understand the purpose of each stage.

slides.title: Learning path for Module 14
slides.transcript:
We’ll begin with CSV-style external data and then separate features from the target.

Next, we create training and testing sets, fit a simple classifier, measure performance, compare the model with a baseline, make a new prediction, and discuss leakage.

[tts-break]

The final example puts the main stages together in one compact workflow.

slides.title: Read external-style data
slides.transcript:
Many analytics projects begin with a CSV file. In this browser example, the CSV content is stored as text so the lesson can run without uploading a file.

StringIO makes that text behave like a file, and Pandas read_csv converts it into a DataFrame.

[tts-break]

The table has two input columns—hours and practice—and one outcome column called passed.

In a real project, the same read_csv call could point to an actual file path.

slides.title: Inputs and target
slides.transcript:
Machine learning separates the information used for prediction from the outcome we want to predict.

The input columns are commonly called features and stored in X. The outcome is the target and is commonly stored in y.

Here hours and practice become X, while passed becomes y.

[tts-break]

This separation is conceptually important. The model is allowed to learn from the features. The target is the answer it is trying to learn to predict.

slides.title: Train/test split
slides.transcript:
A model should be evaluated on data it did not use for learning.

Make_classification creates a small synthetic dataset. Train_test_split then places seventy-five percent of the rows in the training set and twenty-five percent in the test set.

With eighty rows total, that gives sixty training rows and twenty test rows.

[tts-break]

Random_state keeps the split reproducible so we get the same rows each time we run the example.

The test set acts as unseen data for evaluation.

slides.title: Train a simple classifier
slides.transcript:
Now we fit a logistic regression classifier.

The training features and training labels are passed to model dot fit. That is the stage where the model learns patterns from the training data.

After fitting, predict is used on the first five test rows to produce class predictions.

[tts-break]

At this point, seeing predictions is not enough. We still need to compare them with the true test labels to know whether the model is performing well.

slides.title: Evaluate predictions
slides.transcript:
Evaluation compares model predictions with the correct answers in the test set.

Accuracy is the proportion of predictions that are correct. The confusion matrix gives more detail by separating correct and incorrect predictions for each class.

[tts-break]

Do not rely on accuracy alone in every problem. If one class is rare, a model can look accurate while still performing poorly on the cases that matter.

For this introductory example, focus on understanding that evaluation must happen on unseen data.

slides.title: Compare with a baseline
slides.transcript:
A machine learning model should be compared with a simple reference point.

The DummyClassifier uses a basic strategy: always predict the most frequent class. That gives us baseline accuracy with almost no intelligence.

Logistic regression is then evaluated on the same test data.

[tts-break]

If a more complex model cannot beat a simple baseline, we should question whether the model adds useful predictive value.

Baselines help put performance numbers into context.

slides.title: Predict a new case
slides.transcript:
After training, a model can generate a prediction for a new row—as long as the new row has the same feature structure used during training.

The example contains four feature values because the model was trained with four input features. Predict returns the class, and predict_proba returns estimated class probabilities.

[tts-break]

The largest probability is printed as a confidence-like value, but remember that a probability estimate is not a guarantee.

New data must be prepared in the same way as the training data.

slides.title: Avoid leakage
slides.transcript:
Data leakage happens when the model receives information during training that would not truly be available when making a future prediction.

A direct example would be accidentally including the target itself—or a variable derived from the future answer—inside the feature set.

[tts-break]

Leakage can make evaluation look unrealistically strong. Split data before final evaluation, keep target information out of the features, and make sure cleaning steps are applied consistently without using test information improperly.

A model is only useful if its evaluation resembles the conditions in which it will actually be used.

slides.title: Mini ML workflow
slides.transcript:
This final example puts the main modeling steps into one sequence.

A synthetic dataset is created, then split into training and test sets. A decision tree with maximum depth three is fitted on the training data. Predictions are generated for the test set, and accuracy is calculated.

[tts-break]

The exact accuracy is less important than the workflow: data, split, train, predict, evaluate.

Change the tree depth or the random state and compare what happens. Small modeling decisions can change performance, which is why reproducibility and evaluation matter.

slides.title: Module 14 wrap-up
slides.transcript:
Let’s finish with the full workflow.

Read the data. Separate features and target. Split before evaluation. Train a model on the training set. Evaluate on unseen test rows. Compare performance with a baseline. Make new predictions carefully, and watch for leakage.

[tts-break]

You now have a first end-to-end machine learning workflow in Python. The next step in a dedicated machine learning course would be deeper work on preprocessing, model selection, validation, metrics, tuning, and responsible deployment.

[tts-break]

This is the final module in the course, so there is not another numbered module after this one. The next step is to bring the full workflow together in your own analytics work: obtain data, prepare it carefully, explore it, summarize it, communicate what you find, and use predictive methods only when they fit the question. The goal is not simply to know individual Python commands, but to be able to choose and connect the right methods for a complete analytical problem.
